_comment: Single source of truth for everything the Tier B/C container packaging
profiles (apps/truenas, apps/unraid, apps/openmediavault, and any later
profile that wraps the same image) have to agree on. WP4.3's REFACTOR
step asks for exactly this: the three platforms' metadata is generated
from and checked against one file instead of drifting independently.
apps/common/packaging's test suite fails the build if any platform's
own metadata disagrees with a value in here.

note: published:false is the honest state, matching container/release-manifest.json's
own note: no registry is configured for this repository yet, so this reference
resolves to nothing today. It is the intended publish target and the one string
every provider package must carry, so that pointing the project at a real
registry is a one-line change here rather than an edit in four metadata formats.
Every acceptance procedure in docs/acceptance/ opens with a step 0 covering how
to make the image resolvable in the meantime (push to your own registry, or
docker save/load), and every profile keeps the reference substitutable.

truenas.hostPathNote: tank is the pool name the defaults assume; docs/acceptance/truenas-provider-acceptance.md step 0.2 covers substituting a real pool.
truenas.trustForwardedHeadersNote: The catalog entry and the paste-in compose both declare their own project network, created and destroyed with the deployment, whose only two members are these two containers. The Web UI container is the engine's sole possible direct TCP peer by topology, which is what apps/common/auth/local requires.

unraid.hostPathNote: appdata holds private state, and retained artifacts land in a directory of the app's own inside the backups user share; §19.2 keeps those two separate security domains. The backup root is deliberately a dedicated child of the share rather than the share itself: the share is very likely to be one the operator already uses, and step 0 of the acceptance procedure creates and owns only paths it created.
unraid.trustForwardedHeadersNote: Unraid's two templates join `backup-manager`, a durable, host-wide, generically named user-defined bridge the operator creates by hand. Every container on such a bridge reaches every port of every other one, so the engine's isolation from anything else attached later is a convention, not a topology, and apps/common/auth/local requires a topology. The engine therefore does not trust forwarded headers here and rate-limits on the proxy's own address: one shared bucket for all clients, which over-limits rather than not limiting at all. This is the one place the Unraid profile is weaker than the compose ones, and apps/unraid/README.md says so.

openmediavault.hostPathNote: dev-disk-by-uuid is a placeholder, deliberately matching what apps/openmediavault/frontend/platform.ts already declares: a real OMV system mounts data filesystems at /srv/dev-disk-by-uuid-<UUID>/, which differs per machine. The profile funnels every host path through the one DISK variable so the UUID is substituted exactly once, and the compose file derives the rest. Retained artifacts land in a dedicated child of the backups directory rather than in the directory itself, so step 0 of the acceptance procedure only ever creates and owns paths it created.
openmediavault.trustForwardedHeadersNote: The compose file declares its own project network, created and destroyed with the deployment, whose only two members are these two containers.

proxmox.hostPathNote: These are paths inside the GUEST, not on the Proxmox VE host. WP4.5 rules out running the app on the host, so the supported model is a dedicated container-host guest (a VM by default) with one PVE host directory or dataset shared into it at /mnt/backup-manager. How that sharing is configured is the operator's choice (virtiofs, NFS, or pct --mp0 for the LXC variant) and is therefore documented rather than declared here.
